assertion: a library card — A library card links a borrower to their library account and loans.
an audiobook — An audiobook is a spoken recording of a book or other written work.
a bookworm — Bookworm is a familiar figurative name for an enthusiastic reader.
an e-reader — An e-reader is designed mainly for storing and reading electronic books.
a dust jacket — A dust jacket protects a hardback and usually carries its title and cover artwork.
Bram Stoker — Bram Stoker published his famous Gothic vampire novel in 1897.
Mario Puzo — Mario Puzo wrote the crime novel about the Corleone family.
John Grisham — John Grisham became known for bestselling novels set around lawyers and courtrooms.
Michael Ende — Michael Ende wrote the fantasy adventure about Bastian and the world of Fantastica.
Ken Follett — Ken Follett writes historical epics and thrillers, including both of these bestselling novels.
The Old Man and the Sea — Santiago hooks an enormous marlin after a long run of unsuccessful fishing.

supportingSource.title: The Old Man and the Sea — Wikipedia

assertion: The Alchemist — Santiago's journey toward the pyramids becomes a story about pursuing a personal dream.
The Book Thief — Markus Zusak's novel has Death narrate Liesel's life and her love of stolen books.
The Girl on the Train — Paula Hawkins's thriller begins when Rachel's daily view from the train draws her into a mystery.

supportingSource.title: The Girl on the Train (novel) — Wikipedia

assertion: Madame Bovary — Emma Bovary seeks excitement beyond her marriage, with disastrous consequences.
a haiku — Modern English-language haiku commonly use three lines, while Japanese haiku may appear in a single line.
a nursery rhyme — Nursery rhymes are short traditional verses shared with young children.
a poetry slam — A poetry slam combines performed verse with judging by a panel or audience members.
spoken word — Spoken word poetry centres on live recitation, using voice and intonation as expressive tools.
an elegy — An elegy is a poem of mourning or solemn reflection, often written for the dead.
a dress rehearsal — A dress rehearsal runs the production much as the audience will later see it.
a standing ovation — During a standing ovation, spectators stand while showing their approval with applause.
an understudy — An understudy prepares to take over a particular role when the usual performer is unavailable.
stage directions — Stage directions appear alongside dialogue and can specify entrances, exits and how lines are delivered.
a curtain call — During a curtain call, the cast returns to receive the audience's applause.
a happy ending — A happy ending resolves the central conflict positively for the main characters.
a flashback — A flashback moves the narrative back in time to reveal earlier events.
a prequel — A prequel is released after another work but tells events that occur earlier.
a cliffhanger — A cliffhanger delays the resolution so the audience wants to know what happens next.
a red herring — A red herring sends readers or viewers toward a false conclusion.
Obelix — Obelix delivers menhirs and joins Asterix in resisting the Romans.
Tinker Bell — Tinker Bell accompanies Peter Pan and communicates through the sound of bells.
Baloo — Baloo is Mowgli's bear teacher and friend in The Jungle Book.
Captain Haddock — Captain Haddock joins Tintin on many adventures and is known for colourful outbursts.
Snufkin — Snufkin values freedom, travels south each winter and returns to Moominvalley in spring.
a pronoun — Pronouns refer to people or things without repeating their names.
an adverb — Adverbs commonly add information about manner, time, place or degree.
a proper noun — Names such as Maria and Tallinn are proper nouns rather than general labels.
an auxiliary verb — An auxiliary verb works with a main verb, as have does in have finished.
the comparative degree — The comparative degree compares two things, often by adding -er in English.

supportingSource.title: Degrees of comparison of adjectives and adverbs — Wikipedia

assertion: the Celsius scale — The scale is named after Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius, who proposed its first version in 1742.
the volt — The SI unit honours Alessandro Volta, an early pioneer of electrical science.

assertion: the Richter scale — Charles Richter helped develop the magnitude scale that became associated with his surname.
the Heimlich manoeuvre — The technique uses abdominal thrusts to help clear an obstructed airway.
the Beaufort scale — The Beaufort scale links numbered wind force to observable conditions at sea or on land.
a capital letter — Capital letters mark sentence beginnings and proper names in English and Estonian.
an exclamation mark — An exclamation mark ends an exclamation and can add emphasis.
a percent sign — The percent sign shows that a number is expressed as a fraction of one hundred.
a hyphen — A hyphen joins words or word parts and is shorter than a dash.
an underscore — An underscore is written below the usual text baseline and is common in computing.
Journey to the Centre of the Earth — The travellers descend through Snæfellsjökull and discover a vast underground world.

supportingSource.title: Journey to the Centre of the Earth — Wikipedia

assertion: The Prince and the Pauper — Prince Edward and the poor boy Tom Canty exchange clothes and are mistaken for one another.

supportingSource.title: The Prince and the Pauper — Wikipedia

assertion: Doctor Zhivago — Yuri Zhivago's personal life unfolds amid revolution and civil war in Russia.
The Kite Runner — The novel links Amir and Hassan's friendship to Afghanistan's turbulent modern history.
Sophie's World — Jostein Gaarder's novel combines Sophie's story with an introduction to major philosophers.
J. K. Rowling — J. K. Rowling wrote the novel series about Harry's years at Hogwarts.
Enid Blyton — Enid Blyton created both groups of young adventurers in long-running book series.
Louisa May Alcott — Louisa May Alcott is best known for writing Little Women and its sequels.
Frances Hodgson Burnett — Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote both enduring children's novels.
Elena Ferrante — Elena Ferrante's four-book series follows the lifelong friendship of Elena and Lila.
All Quiet on the Western Front — Erich Maria Remarque's novel depicts the physical and emotional strain of trench warfare.

supportingSource.title: All Quiet on the Western Front — Wikipedia

assertion: A Clockwork Orange — Alex narrates the violent dystopian story in a distinctive invented vocabulary.
Memoirs of a Geisha — Arthur Golden's novel tells Sayuri's life story from childhood onward.
The English Patient — Michael Ondaatje's novel gradually uncovers the histories of four people sheltering in the villa.
Flowers for Algernon — Daniel Keyes tells Charlie's story through progress reports that change as the experiment takes effect.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe — Faust is one of Goethe's best-known and most influential works.
Sappho — Sappho was a lyric poet from Lesbos whose verse was originally accompanied by music.
Ovid — Ovid's Metamorphoses is a fifteen-book mythological narrative and a major source for classical myths.
Emily Dickinson — Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems, most of which appeared after her death.
Rumi — Rumi's lyric and narrative poetry has remained influential far beyond the Persian-speaking world.
Grease — Grease pairs Danny and Sandy's romance with 1950s-style songs and dancing.
Starlight Express — The actors play trains on roller skates as the steam engine Rusty competes against modern locomotives.
Evita — Evita dramatises Eva Perón's rise to prominence in Argentina.
The Rocky Horror Show — The stage musical sends Brad and Janet into Frank-N-Furter's strange castle.
Miss Saigon — Miss Saigon centres on the relationship between Kim, a Vietnamese woman, and Chris, an American serviceman.
a biography — A biography is a nonfiction account of a person's life written by another author.
detective fiction — Detective fiction follows clues and reasoning toward an explanation of a crime.
Gothic fiction — Gothic fiction creates suspense through threatening settings, mystery and supernatural possibilities.
melodrama — Melodrama emphasises strong emotion and sharply drawn moral conflict.
tragicomedy — Tragicomedy blends features normally associated with tragedy and comedy.
Bambi — Bambi learns about the forest and its dangers as he grows up.
Gandalf — Gandalf is a wise wizard who opposes Sauron in Tolkien's Middle-earth stories.
Gollum — The Ring has prolonged and twisted Gollum's life, and he is obsessed with recovering it.
Huckleberry Finn — Huckleberry Finn narrates an escape and river journey through the American South.
Long John Silver — Long John Silver is a charismatic ship's cook who secretly leads the pirates.
a proverb — A proverb passes down a compact observation or piece of practical wisdom.
an antonym — Antonyms are words whose meanings contrast with one another.
a cliché — A cliché has lost much of its freshness through overuse.
a homonym — Homonyms have the same form or sound but different meanings.
a euphemism — A euphemism replaces direct wording with something considered less offensive or uncomfortable.
a kiosk — Kiosk passed through Turkish and European languages before taking on its modern retail meaning.
pyjamas — The word entered English through Hindustani, from an Urdu term for leg clothing.
khaki — The word khaki came from Hindustani and was applied to soil-coloured military cloth.
a hammock — Spanish adopted the Taíno word hamaca, which then entered English as hammock.
a kayak — The English word kayak comes from Inuktitut qajaq, the name of the traditional boat.
Arabic numerals — Arabic numerals are the ten digit symbols used for everyday decimal notation.
Comic Sans — Comic Sans was designed for friendly speech-bubble text and later spread widely through computer software.
a monogram — A monogram arranges initials or other letters into a single identifying design.
cursive — Cursive handwriting connects letters so the pen can move smoothly across the page.
blackletter — Blackletter uses tightly packed angular strokes and was widespread in medieval Europe.
Aeolus — Aeolus confines the contrary winds, but Odysseus’s crew opens the bag and blows the ship back off course.
Nausicaa — Nausicaa gives the stranger clothing and directions to the palace of her parents, Alcinous and Arete.
Eumaeus — Eumaeus remains faithful during Odysseus’s absence and joins him and Telemachus in the final fight.
the Laestrygonians — The Laestrygonians hurl rocks from the cliffs and spear the trapped crews, leaving only Odysseus’s ship to escape.
Argus — Argus alone immediately recognizes the returned hero, making their brief reunion a symbol of enduring loyalty.
blank verse — Blank verse keeps a regular metre without end rhyme, allowing speech to sound elevated yet flexible.
soliloquy — A soliloquy makes the character’s inner reasoning audible to the audience rather than to another character.
an aside — An aside creates confidential contact with the audience without stopping the surrounding scene.
groundlings — Groundlings occupied the yard below the galleries and watched performances while standing close to the stage.
the tiring house — The term comes from “attiring”: this backstage building held costumes, entrances, and working space for performers.
an epistolary novel — Epistolary fiction presents the narrative as records made by its characters, often multiplying viewpoints and uncertainty.
a frame story — A frame story surrounds one or more embedded narratives with an outer narrative situation.
an unreliable narrator — The gap between the narrator’s version and what readers infer becomes a central source of tension and interpretation.
a doppelgänger — Gothic and psychological fiction use the double to externalize divided identity, guilt, or a repressed self.
the uncanny — The uncanny troubles the boundary between familiar and foreign, making dolls, doubles, repetitions, or homes feel unsafe.
Cloud Atlas — Mitchell arranges the narratives concentrically: five stop at a turning point, the central story is complete, and the interrupted stories then close in reverse order.
House of Leaves — The page layout becomes part of the labyrinth: text contracts, expands, turns, and fragments as the explorers move through the impossible house.
If on a winter’s night a traveler — Alternating chapters follow the Reader and the Other Reader, while each even-numbered chapter begins a new novel that breaks off before its resolution.

supportingSource.title: If on a winter’s night a traveler

assertion: Pale Fire — The novel’s foreword, poem, commentary, and index force readers to reconstruct the conflict between Shade’s work and Kinbote’s intrusive interpretation.
Hopscotch — Cortázar’s table of instructions creates an alternative sequence that mixes the main narrative with the book’s “expendable” chapters.

assertion: Holden Caulfield — Holden recounts the days after his expulsion in a defensive, conversational voice that exposes both his judgment of others and his own grief.
Scout — The adult Jean Louise Finch narrates events largely through the perspective of her younger self, Scout.
Nick Carraway — Nick is both Gatsby’s neighbour and Daisy’s cousin, placing him inside the relationships whose collapse he records.
Saleem Sinai — Saleem ties the story of his body and family to the history of independent India while addressing his account to Padma.
Stevens — Stevens’s carefully controlled recollections gradually expose the personal cost of his devotion to service and dignity.
Psyche — The underworld errand is the last of Venus’s impossible tasks for Psyche before divine help leads to her reunion with Cupid.
the Cumaean Sibyl — The Sibyl serves as Aeneas’s authorized guide after the golden bough opens the way into the realm below.
Izanagi — Izanagi seals the entrance to Yomi after his failed rescue and then purifies himself from contact with death.
Inanna — Inanna arrives stripped of her powers, is killed, and can return only after a substitute is provided.

supportingSource.title: Descent of Inanna into the Underworld

assertion: katabasis — A katabasis is literally a going down and often becomes a journey toward knowledge, transformation, or return.
a villanelle — A villanelle repeats its first and third lines in a fixed pattern before bringing both together at the close.
terza rima — In terza rima, the middle rhyme of one tercet supplies the outer rhyme of the next, producing a continuous chain.
a pantoum — The pantoum’s interlocking repetitions let the same lines gather new meanings as their surroundings change.
a sestina — A sestina substitutes a prescribed permutation of end-words for rhyme and finishes with a short envoi.
ottava rima — Ottava rima’s final couplet can deliver a pointed turn or comic deflation after three alternating rhymes.
Saint Jerome — Jerome revised earlier Latin texts and translated much of the Old Testament from Hebrew.
Edward FitzGerald — FitzGerald reshaped and combined Persian quatrains into an English sequence that became far more famous than its first edition suggested.
Constance Garnett — Garnett’s many translations made Russian fiction broadly available in English despite later debate about her style and omissions.
Arthur Waley — Waley learned classical Chinese and Japanese largely outside academia and brought both literary traditions to a wide English readership.
Gregory Rabassa — Rabassa became a defining English-language voice for the Latin American Boom and translated the Márquez novel without first reading it in full.
Lilliput — Swift gives Lilliput its own capital, court, rival factions, and conflict with neighbouring Blefuscu, making the tiny realm a map-sized political satire.
Ankh-Morpork — Guilds, civic institutions, and a famously pragmatic ruler make Ankh-Morpork the political and comic hub of Discworld.
Yoknapatawpha County — Faulkner repeatedly returned to the county’s families and history, modelling its geography on Mississippi’s Lafayette County.
Ruritania — Anthony Hope’s kingdom became so influential that “Ruritanian” can describe later stories set in similar imaginary monarchies.
Gormenghast — The castle is effectively a central character: its endless buildings and ceremonies shape every part of Titus’s inherited life.
quarantena — Italian quarantena and French quarantaine both refer to a period of forty days, the duration used in the historical health measure.
Bengali — The word originally described a house in the Bengal style before becoming a general name for a low house.
great lord — The honorific passed into English and broadened from a powerful ruler to a powerful business magnate.
chāmpo — The borrowed command first referred to massage and only later narrowed toward washing the hair and the product used for it.
berserkr — Old Norse berserkr named one of the legendary warriors whose battle frenzy gave the modern word its sense.
The Tales of Beedle the Bard — Dumbledore leaves the book to Hermione, and its story about three magical gifts reveals the Hallows’ shared legend.

supportingSource.title: The Tales of Beedle the Bard

assertion: the Necronomicon — Lovecraft scattered references to the book across stories, giving his invented mythology the appearance of documentary depth.
the Red Book of Westmarch — The imagined manuscript gives Tolkien’s legendarium a layered history in which hobbits preserve and transmit the account.
The Grasshopper Lies Heavy — Hawthorne Abendsen’s novel within the novel offers the occupied characters a competing history, though it does not exactly match ours.
the Encyclopedia Galactica — Adams uses the grander encyclopedia as a foil for the Guide’s portability, sales, and cheerfully questionable accuracy.
Wide Sargasso Sea — Rhys gives Rochester’s first wife a history and voice of her own, turning a figure from the edge of Jane Eyre into the centre of the story.
Grendel — Gardner makes Grendel the narrator, recasting the epic conflict as the monster’s search for meaning before Beowulf arrives.
The Penelopiad — The novella revisits the Odyssey from the afterlife, questioning both Odysseus’s legend and the maids’ punishment.
A Thousand Acres — Smiley relocates Shakespeare’s family tragedy to a modern farm and shifts sympathy toward the eldest daughter’s perspective.
Hag-Seed — Felix uses the prison production to pursue revenge, echoing Prospero while directing his own version of the play.
The Name of the Rose — William’s inquiry joins a murder mystery to debates about knowledge, laughter, and the control of books.
The Shadow of the Wind — Daniel’s attempt to learn about Carax draws him into a mystery involving someone who is destroying every surviving copy of the author’s books.
Possession — The modern investigation alternates with poems, diaries, and letters attributed to the fictional poets Randolph Ash and Christabel LaMotte.
The Historian — Nested accounts follow generations of researchers across Europe as scholarship becomes a dangerous confrontation with the Dracula legend.
People of the Book — Each physical clue opens a story from the illuminated manuscript’s imagined passage through persecution, exile, and rescue.
The Mystery of Edwin Drood — Dickens died while the serial was in progress, leaving Edwin’s fate and the intended culprit open to debate.
Sanditon — Austen stopped work as her health declined, leaving the resort satire and Charlotte’s story incomplete.
The Good Soldier Švejk — Hašek completed only part of his planned comic sequence, so Švejk never reaches a conventional conclusion.
Dead Souls — Gogol envisioned further parts but destroyed much of the continuation, leaving the satirical project unfinished.
The Original of Laura — The published volume preserves Nabokov’s movable cards and fragments rather than presenting a completed novel.
Noises Off — The revolving set exposes how the actors’ quarrels and missed cues turn the play within the play into chaos.
Six Characters in Search of an Author — The characters insist that their drama is more real than the actors’ imitation, blurring rehearsal, performance, and reality.

supportingSource.title: Six Characters in Search of an Author

assertion: The Real Inspector Hound — Stoppard parodies both formula mysteries and reviewing as the observers become characters in the play they are watching.
The Dresser — The wartime theatre company depends on the intimate, unequal bond between the aging actor-manager and the dresser who sustains him.
Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead — Rosencrantz and Guildenstern move between Shakespeare’s familiar scenes and an absurdist uncertainty they cannot escape.
quixotic — The adjective derives from Don Quixote and describes noble but impractical idealism.
utopia — More’s book made Utopia the name of an imagined commonwealth, and the word became a general term for an ideal but unreal society.
pandemonium — Milton formed Pandæmonium as the demons’ assembly place; the name later broadened to any scene of uproar and disorder.
yahoo — Swift’s Yahoos embody degraded human appetites, and their name entered English for a loutish or uncivilized person.
chortle — Carroll’s portmanteau outgrew the poem and became an ordinary English verb and noun for a delighted laugh.
The Unknown Soldier — Linna’s ensemble of conscripts presents the war from the ranks and became a central work of Finnish post-war literature.
The Summer Book — The island conversations let childhood curiosity and old age meet against weather, sea, and the family’s quiet grief.
Kristin Lavransdatter — Kristin’s choices, faith, and bond with Erlend unfold across The Wreath, The Wife, and The Cross.
Growth of the Soil — Isak’s homestead anchors a novel about labour, settlement, family, and the pressure of modern change.
Independent People — Bjartur’s refusal to depend on others gives him dignity but also drives the losses at the heart of the Icelandic novel.
The Diary of a Young Girl — Frank wrote while hiding with her family during the Nazi occupation; her father Otto later prepared the diary for publication.

supportingSource.title: The Diary of a Young Girl

When Breath Becomes Air — Kalanithi writes from both sides of medicine, moving from treating patients to facing mortality as a patient himself.
O Captain! My Captain! — Whitman turns the end of the Civil War into a victorious voyage overshadowed by the captain’s death.
The New Colossus — Lines from the poem were mounted inside the statue’s pedestal and helped define the monument as a symbol of welcome.
In Flanders Fields — McCrae gives the fallen soldiers a collective voice from the fields where the living are urged to continue their cause.
If— — The poem frames maturity as self-command under pressure and ends by promising that these qualities make the listener a man.
Dulce et Decorum est — Owen uses a soldier’s choking death to expose the patriotic Latin motto as “the old Lie.”
Coraline — Coraline discovers that the tempting copy of her home is a trap and must rescue both her parents and other imprisoned children.
A Wrinkle in Time — The children cross space with Mrs Whatsit, Mrs Who, and Mrs Which to confront enforced sameness on Camazotz.
The Phantom Tollbooth — Milo’s journey through wordplay and number puzzles leads him to rescue the princesses Rhyme and Reason.
Inkheart — Mo’s gift exchanges people between fiction and reality, and the family must face the characters he accidentally released.
The Dark Is Rising — Will’s familiar English countryside opens into an ancient struggle between the Light and the Dark.
The Importance of Being Earnest — Wilde’s title pun and the heroes’ invented lives drive a satire of courtship, respectability, and social convention.
Pygmalion — Eliza’s transformation exposes how accent and manners act as gates to class, while she demands control over her own future.
The Government Inspector — Khlestakov accepts bribes and admiration while the frightened officials expose their own dishonesty.
The Imaginary Invalid — The play mocks credulous patients and pompous medicine as Argan’s household stages schemes to cure him of manipulation rather than disease.
The Servant of Two Masters — Truffaldino’s attempt to double his wages and food multiplies disguises, crossed messages, and physical comedy.
Eat, Pray, Love — Gilbert explores personal renewal through three contrasting cultures; the Indonesian part takes place on Bali.

Hotel du Lac — Edith observes the other guests while deciding whether to accept a respectable but loveless future.
Grand Hotel — The hotel’s revolving population lets Baum cross several lives in a portrait of Weimar-era Berlin.
The Hotel New Hampshire — The family repeatedly rebuilds its idea of home amid accidents, loss, theatrical schemes, and improbable hotel ventures.
